title: The Rise of Artificial Intelligence in Educational Measurement: Opportunities and Ethical Challenges
extended_summary:
This white paper examines how artificial intelligence, including generative AI and large language models, is being incorporated into educational measurement and assessment. Rather than testing a single intervention, it surveys major application areas such as automated item generation, multimodal stimulus generation, automated scoring, and AI-supported score reporting and feedback, while emphasizing the ethical and psychometric issues that arise in each area.

The paper focuses on how AI tools can support assessment workflows by generating items, producing feedback, and scoring constructed responses more efficiently and at scale. It discusses implementation requirements such as human-in-the-loop oversight, multidisciplinary collaboration, representative training data, prompt engineering, transparency, explainability, and privacy protections. It also uses illustrative examples from AP Chinese Language and Culture and NAEP scoring challenges to show where AI and human judgments align or diverge.

The paper does not study a single classroom population or a specific K-12 intervention; instead, it is a conceptual and policy-oriented synthesis aimed at researchers, assessment specialists, educators, and policymakers. Its main conclusion is that AI can improve assessment efficiency and responsiveness, but only when used with careful validation, fairness checks, and strong human oversight. The authors argue that responsible deployment requires attention to bias, accountability, accessibility, and the educational purpose of the assessment system.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot used for text generation, scoring, and feedback-related tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in an illustrative example to score AP Chinese writing responses, alongside a human rater, and to provide scoring rationales for those responses.

findings.finding_summary: In an illustrative comparison using 30 essay samples from 30 third-year college students, ChatGPT 3.5 and 4.0 produced scoring rationales that were internally consistent, but their scoring method differed from the human rater's. The paper reports that ChatGPT evaluated each rubric criterion independently and averaged the scores, whereas the human rater used a holistic approach; this methodological difference could lead to a different score distribution. No formal effect size or inferential test was reported.
findings.measure: AP Chinese writing scores and scoring rationales on a 0-6 scale

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI / large language model tools broadly used to generate text, items, feedback, and automated scoring outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as a class of tools across automated item generation, multimodal stimulus generation, automated scoring, feedback enhancement, and automated writing evaluation; the paper synthesizes ethical considerations and implementation conditions rather than evaluating one generic tool empirically.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a white paper / conceptual review with one illustrative example and no rigorous empirical study design reported for the paper as a whole. The evidence is therefore not suitable for higher-confidence causal inference.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper describes potentially meaningful uses and implementation conditions for generative AI, but it does not report robust effect estimates for the paper's main claims. The only quantitative example is descriptive and provides no effect size.
